scholarly_argument_bobzien_autexousion_a.description: Bobzien's n. 55 (p. 164) states that exousia — not autexousion — does not occur in the relevant kind of account of 'what depends on us' in Aspasius, the Anonymous, Alcinous, [Plutarch] On Fate, 'nor in Justin and Tatian'; she makes no claim about autexousion in Justin or Tatian. scholarly_argument_bobzien_eph_hemin_wha.description: Bobzien (1998, pp. 139-141) distinguishes two senses of the Greek 'depending on someone': a 'one-sided, causative' concept ('attributable to us', naming who bears causal responsibility — the Stoic use) and a 'two-sided, potestative' concept ('up to us': if x depends on us, so does not-x), well attested in Greek and, philosophically, 'based on Aristotle's ethics'. The two-sided potestative eph' hemin 'itself entails neither determinism nor indeterminism'; only on an indeterminist reading does it imply freedom to do otherwise. The 'In conclusion…' quote belongs to Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy (2001), p. 412, not to the article.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_exousia_and_c.description: Bobzien conjectures ('I can only offer conjecture', p. 164) that Alexander's replacement of dynasthai by exousia — used by him as virtually synonymous with being kyrios over something — 'may have been of great significance', since it provided a way to express that the agent is 'a causally undetermined decision maker', and is 'one further step towards the concept of a free will'. This holds only 'at least at times' (n. 58: the exousia phrase can also mean being unhindered, or a general two-sided capacity). The contrast is with Aristotle and Epictetus, for whom control meant that nothing hindered us (pp. 164-166).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_greek_termino.description: Bobzien notes that the only proper Greek term for freedom is eleutheria and that 'our evidence suggests' it played no role in the discussion of determinism and moral responsibility up to the 2nd century A.D.; in particular it is not involved in the development of the concept of freedom to do otherwise. The pertinent development is that of the phrase eph' hemin ('depending on us'), which has 'an altogether different history'; eleutheria later becomes connected with autonomous agency and with freedoms of types 5-7 (p. 135). 'Up to us' is, for her, the translation fitting only the two-sided potestative reading (p. 140).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_historical_ma.description: Bobzien warns against assuming that at the turn of the 2nd century a general awareness of the problem of causal determinism and freedom to do otherwise had arisen: Alexander 'is almost an isolated case', and concepts of freedom to do otherwise are 'a rather marginal phenomenon without a clear philosophical context'. The one-sided causative eph' hemin was 'by no means peculiar to the Stoic system' and seems to have been regarded as 'a serious alternative or as a complement' to the two-sided potestative conception in 2nd-3rd century Middle-Platonist and Peripatetic writings (p. 167); the problem 'was not part of the philosophical repertoire for long' (p. 175).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_middle_platon.description: On Bobzien's reconstruction, an 'Aristotle scholar' behind the Middle-Platonist common source — 'equally well a Peripatetic or a Platonist' (p. 148) — subordinated what depends on us to the contingent ('in equal parts'), combining EN III.3, De Int. 13 and De Int. 9 (pp. 147-152); Alcinous and Ammonius may show a step towards undeterminedness (pp. 154-155), but she leaves open whether Middle-Platonists read it as causal indeterminism (p. 156). Exousia is absent from Alcinous and [Plutarch] On Fate: Alexander seems the first known to use it in such accounts (p. 164 n. 55); autexousion is linked to Epictetus and late-2nd-century usage (pp. 166-167).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_middle_platon.finding: Two of three elements contradict Bobzien. (1) 'introducing notions of power (exousia, dynamis, autexousion)': she argues the reverse — exousia is NOT found in Alcinous or [Plutarch] On Fate (n. 55, p. 164) and 'Alexander seems to be the first – of whom we know – to use the term' in such accounts (p. 164, file lines 1508-1510); the Middle-Platonist account uses only 'being capable of' (dynasthai), which Alexander later replaces; autexousion is tied to Epictetus and to late-2nd-century usage (pp. 166-167), not to the Middle-Platonist fate doctrine. Her one Middle-Platonist exousia witness, Maximus of Tyre, concerns how vice entered the world, not accounts of what depends on us (p. 165). (2) 'Middle-Platonists contributed ... by linking contingency with eph' hemin': faithful to sections VI-VII, but Bobzien attributes the passage to an 'Aristotle scholar' who 'could be equally well a Peripatetic or a Platonist' (p. 148). The Alcinous Greek in verified_reference is quoted by Bobzien (p. 154, legacy encoding) but plays no role in the node's claims.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_moral_respons.description: Bobzien distinguishes two 'categorically different conceptions of moral responsibility': MR1, grounded on the autonomy of the agent (it was the agent and not something else that was causally responsible), and MR2, requiring that the agent could have done otherwise (p. 135). MR1 is the position of the Stoics in Alexander (pp. 137, 141); MR2 'appears to be Alexander's own position' (p. 142), although he vacillates: the link between freedom of decision and MR2 appears 'finally' in the regret argument (p. 170), and he treats freedom to do otherwise as a prerequisite for responsibility only 'at least at times' (p. 172).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_types_of_free.description: Bobzien's opening distinctions — 'kept rough and schematic' and 'deliberately vague' — separate three kinds of indeterminist freedom (freedom to do otherwise; freedom of decision, its subtype; freedom of the will, a subtype requiring a faculty of the will) from 'un-predeterminist' freedom (no prior determining causes, yet the same agent in the same circumstances would always choose the same), and from three freedoms compatible with both: from force and compulsion, from determination by external causal factors, and from (external and) certain internal causal factors. Indeterminist and un-predeterminist freedom are 'often confounded' in reading ancient texts; the list is 'neither exhaustive nor exclusive' (pp. 133-134).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_chrysippus_co.description: In the Diogenianus/Eusebius report Chrysippus distinguishes occurrents 'fated simply or in isolation' from occurrents 'fated together with' some human activity; the things that happen because of us are 'fated-along-with' the administration of the universe. The co-fated occurrent stands to the action as to a necessary condition ('it cannot happen without us wanting it to happen and making an effort'), and those actions are themselves fated. Bobzien reads this as a refutation of the Idle Argument preserving intentional action within fate-determinism — 'not a defence of free-will'; moral responsibility is a separate problem (ch. 6).

evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:8520-8523] (Bobzien 1998, p. 181)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_chrysippus_mo.description: Chrysippus' modal notions (a minimal modification of Diodorus' possibility, with Philo's criterion added) preserve counterfactual possibilities and so secure 'an adequate modal basis' for purposeful action and the attribution of responsibility. Bobzien stresses that there is 'no direct evidence that Chrysippus linked his modal theory to his doctrine of fate'; from his denial that everything fated is necessary she infers that, on his own modal notions, not everything fated comes out as necessary. Opponents alleged an inconsistency; Chrysippus' reply distinguishes cosmological Necessity from the modal 'that which is necessary' (§3.4).

evidence.quote: We have no direct evidence that Chrysippus linked his modal theory to his doctrine of fate. But we know that he denied that everything that is fated is also necessary.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:5844-5846] (Bobzien 1998, p. 122)

evidence.quote: From this I believe we can infer that he thought that, at least according to his own modal notions, not everything fated comes out as necessary

scholarly_argument_bobzien_chrysippus_mo.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 5840-5846 (p. 122, §3.2). The node states that Chrysippus' modal system is 'based on his distinction between fate and necessity' and 'resolves' the conflict. Bobzien is more cautious: the modal system is built by modifying Diodorus' and Philo's notions (§3.1); 'We have no direct evidence that Chrysippus linked his modal theory to his doctrine of fate'; the fate/necessity non-identity is an inference she draws ('I believe we can infer'), and the terminological distinction between Necessity and 'that which is necessary' is treated separately in §3.4 as a reply to opponents who 'mixed up' the two. page_range 'Chapter 3' = pp. 97-143.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_divination_an.description: Chrysippus proved fate through the existence of divination (§2.2). Against the objection that divination and Stoic contingency are incompatible, Bobzien argues that divinatory theorems (universal, e.g. birth at the rise of Sirius / not dying at sea) 'do not connect causes with effects' but 'connect signs ... with future facts': they express regularity of occurrents, not active causation. She distinguishes these from 'conditional predictions' (prophecies addressed to an individual whose antecedent is the addressee's future action), which the Stoics did treat as causally relevant and fitted into the causal network of fate (§4.2.5).

evidence.quote: Conditional predictions crucially differ from divinatory theorems in that (i) they are signs,75 (ii) they are not universal, but address a particular individual (or a group of individuals), and (iii) their antecedent concerns a future action of the addressee of the prediction.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:8333-8336] (Bobzien 1998, p. 176)

evidence.quote: another kind of divinatory sign, which even the Stoics considered to be causally relevant to what happens in the future. These are divinatory predictions, mostly pro- phecies, which are at least covertly of conditional form.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:8322-8325] (Bobzien 1998, pp. 175-176)

evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:7893-7895] (Bobzien 1998, p. 166)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_divination_an.finding: No quote_verbatim. The sign-relation half is faithful (§4.2 'active causation versus regularity of occurrents', p. 166). But the node conflates Bobzien's two categories: its example 'if someone is born under a certain sign, they will have certain traits' is what she calls a divinatory THEOREM (universal, a sign-relation), whereas her 'conditional predictions' (§4.2.5 Appendix, pp. 175-179) are prophecies addressed to a particular individual whose antecedent is a future action of the addressee, and which the Stoics DID regard as causally relevant. 'Absolute predictions' is not her term; she says theorems 'do not predict the future categorically'. The Chrysippean proof from divination is ch. 2, §2.2 (pp. 87-96), not 59-96 as a whole.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_epictetus_on_.description: For Epictetus, as for the early Stoa, freedom is 'a moral quality which only wise people possess', opposed to slavery and linked to persons and their states of mind rather than to actions. Unlike the early Stoics, Epictetus expressly connects freedom with that which depends on us: one is free if, knowing what depends on one, one never desires or deplores anything that does not. Bobzien adds that Epictetus avoided fate qua network of causes and shows 'no signs of any critical awareness of the problem of compatibilism'; his notion is not concerned with indeterminist freedom either.

evidence.quote: As in the early Stoa, so in Epictetus, freedom is a moral quality which only wise people possess, and it is frequently opposed to slavery
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:15911-15912] (Bobzien 1998, p. 342)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_epictetus_on_.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 15911-15929 (p. 342, §7.2.2). The first two clauses paraphrase Bobzien acceptably ('freedom is a moral quality which only wise people possess'; freedom = not desiring or deploring what does not depend on you). But 'within a compatibilist framework' contradicts her: she says Epictetus 'shows no signs of any critical awareness of the problem of compatibilism', 'avoided talking about fate' qua network of causes, and that his notion of what depends on us is 'not concerned with indeterminist freedom of decision or freedom to do otherwise' — i.e. neutral, not compatibilist. page_range 204-211 is wrong (ch. 5 material); ch. 7 = pp. 330-357.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_epictetus_on_.description: Epictetus places in the class of things that depend on us 'primarily — or perhaps even exclusively — the "use of impressions"', i.e. our assents and the impulses and beliefs that follow from assenting; everything else (actions, results, indifferents, the impressions themselves) does not depend on us. Bobzien reads this as a change of function and perspective: in Chrysippus the notion belonged to physics/psychology and served, backward-looking, the attribution of responsibility; in Epictetus it belongs to ethics and serves, forward-looking, the guidance of life. Freedom as internal, psychological freedom is already early Stoic.

evidence.quote: The perspective from which that which depends on us is discussed has thus become a per- spective towards the future, concerned with guidance of actions and behaviour; before, in Chrysippus and the old Stoa it primarily was a back- wards perspective or time independent, concerned with the attribution of responsibility
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:15491-15496] (Bobzien 1998, p. 333)

evidence.quote: Stoic freedom is thus internal or psychological freedom, i.e. it depends entirely on the state of the mind of the person
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:15865-15867] (Bobzien 1998, p. 341, on the early Stoics)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_epictetus_on_.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 15497-15502 (p. 333). The restriction of what depends on us to the 'use of impressions' (assents, impulses, beliefs) is faithful. But 'a shift toward internalization of freedom' is not Bobzien's characterization: internal/psychological freedom is for her already the early Stoic (indeed pre-Stoic philosophical) notion (pp. 339, 341). The shift she actually describes is one of function and perspective — from a backward-looking notion in physics/psychology preserving responsibility to a forward-looking practical notion within ethics — plus the restriction of range. page_range 331-357 is acceptable (ch. 7 starts p. 330).

scholarly_argument_bobzien_origen_s_resp.description: Bobzien uses three passages as sources for Chrysippus' reply to the Idle Argument: Cicero, On Fate 30 (who names Chrysippus), Origen, Against Celsus II 20, 342.71-82, and Eusebius, Praep. ev. 6.8.25-38. She treats Origen's as 'one incomplete version of a rebuttal', 'something like a refutation' — a parabolic refutation by analogy plus one explanatory sentence — for which Origen 'names neither source nor author' and which may derive from texts later than Chrysippus; 'their reliability as sources for Chrysippus' reply varies'.

evidence.quote: There are further one incomplete version of a rebuttal in Origen (Cels. II 20, 342.71—82) and another in Seneca (Nat. quaest. II 37.3—38.4). Both make points related to Chrysippus' and both could be Stoic, although they may have been taken from texts later than Chrysippus
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:8516-8520] (Bobzien 1998, p. 181)

evidence.quote: But since Origen's report of the argument, too, is followed by something like a refutation (Cels. II 20, 342.71—82), it seems natural to look for further information there. As often, Origen names neither source nor author.68
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:9640-9643] (Bobzien 1998, p. 205)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_origen_s_resp.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 9349-9355 (p. 199, opening of §5.2). page_range 205-208 correctly marks §5.2.2 on Origen (the verified_reference's 'p. 173' is wrong). Bobzien does use Origen as one of her three sources, but she qualifies it heavily: 'one incomplete version of a rebuttal', possibly from texts later than Chrysippus, 'something like a refutation', with Origen naming 'neither source nor author'; the three sources' 'reliability ... varies'. The node's 'one of the key ancient replies' drops these reservations.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_stoic_determi.description: Bobzien presents Chrysippus' determinism as combining teleological determinism (the world rationally ordered by the active principle) with causal determinism (every motion predetermined by antecedent causes within the causal network of fate), and not as naive fatalism, logical determinism or necessitarianism; it is meant to be compatible with 'reasonable concepts of contingency, action, and moral responsibility'. She denies that Chrysippus presupposed empirically detectable 'laws of nature'. The early Stoic problem is not the modern free-will problem: concepts of freedom to do otherwise arise only in later antiquity (§8.7).

evidence.quote: Our text, it seems to me, suggests that in his refutation Chrysippus did not refer to or presuppose any concept of empirically detectable 'laws of nature' or any other type of restricted-scope 'universal relations'.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:10560-10563] (Bobzien 1998, p. 225)

evidence.quote: As in the case of Chrysippus, there is nowhere a clue that PHILOPATOR had a plurality of empirically detectable laws of nature in mind.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:17322-17324] (Bobzien 1998, p. 372)

evidence.quote: Concepts of freedom to do otherwise were developed in later antiquity in the guise of notions of that which depends on us
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:18467-18468] (Bobzien 1998, p. 397)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_stoic_determi.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 794-800 (p. 12). Most of the description is faithful (teleological + causal, not necessitarianism; compatible with contingency and moral responsibility; no free will / freedom to do otherwise — p. 338, 349, §8.7 p. 397: 'Concepts of freedom to do otherwise were developed in later antiquity'). But 'in a law-governed universe' contradicts Bobzien, who repeatedly denies that Chrysippus or PHILOPATOR presupposed empirically detectable 'laws of nature' (pp. 225, 372); at most she allows 'in modern parlance' enormously complex laws governing whole world states with a single instantiation. page_range 'Chapters 1-2' (pp. 16-96) does not contain the quoted p. 12.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_stoic_modal_l.description: Chrysippus was acquainted with both Philo's (conceptual or essentialist) and Diodorus' modal notions; he designed his own 'in contrast with those of Diodorus' while 'somehow incorporat[ing] Philo's', combining the two with only a minimal change to Diodorus' concept of possibility. The resulting system 'escapes Diodorus' necessitarian consequences' by preserving counterfactual possibilities and 'provides an adequate base for his own compatibilism'.

evidence.quote: he designed his own in contrast with those of Diodorus and that he somehow incorporated Philo's. In fact, he combined Philo's and Diodorus' modal notions in a very astute way, making only a minimal change to Diodorus' concept of possibility
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:4694-4697] (Bobzien 1998, p. 98)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_stoic_modal_l.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 4692-4698 (p. 98, §3.1.1). The node says the system is 'distinct from both Diodorus's necessitarianism and Philo's conceptual modalities'; Bobzien says Chrysippus designed his notions 'in contrast with those of Diodorus' but 'somehow incorporated Philo's' — indeed 'combined Philo's and Diodorus' modal notions', adding Philo's account as a first criterion (p. 116 n. 46). 'Conceptual modalities' is her heading (§3.1.3). page_range 133-148 is wrong (§3.3-4.1); §3.1 = pp. 97-121.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_stoic_modal_l.description: Chrysippus' modal system preserves counterfactual possibilities and hence contingency within his determinism (§3.1). Against the charge that 'everything is fated' plus 'fate is Necessity' yields 'everything is necessary', Bobzien reconstructs a Chrysippean distinction between a cosmological concept — Necessity, the universal physical power already equated with Fate by Zeno — and a logical one, 'that which is necessary', one of the four modalities; opponents 'mixed up the terminology and realms of the concepts' (§3.4). The simply-fated / co-fated distinction is a separate matter, from the reply to the Idle Argument (ch. 5).

evidence.quote: Chrysippus had a cosmological and a logical concept of necessity; these two concepts had both different origins and different realms of application and were also referred to by different expressions, although these expressions share the same linguistic root.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:6502-6505] (Bobzien 1998, p. 136)

evidence.quote: Chrysippus' opponents mixed up the terminology and realms of the concepts.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:6508-6509] (Bobzien 1998, p. 136)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_stoic_modal_l.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 6501-6509 (p. 136, §3.4). Two losses: (a) Bobzien's distinction is between a 'cosmological' concept (Necessity, 'the universal physical power' equated with Fate by Zeno) and a 'logical' one ('that which is necessary', one of the four modalities); 'necessity/compulsion' is not her gloss. (b) The 'simply fated' vs 'co-fated' distinction is not part of the modal system at all — it belongs to the reply to the Idle Argument (ch. 5, pp. 211-212, 217-226). page_range 97-143 = ch. 3 is fine for the modal part only.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_the_idle_argu.description: The Idle Argument is 'levelled against fate-determinism': if everything is fated, making an effort is futile. The Stoics treated it as a sophism, and Bobzien finds that it 'contains various sophistic elements'. Chrysippus' refutation — distinguishing occurrents 'fated simply' from those 'fated together with' our actions, which are their necessary conditions — is 'in the first instance just that: a refutation', 'not a defence of free-will'; that which depends on us does not figure in any report of the argument. Yet it yields essential information on his determinism's concepts of causal relevance and intentional action.

evidence.quote: Chrysippus' refutation was countered, in a standard way, by pointing out that it destroys that which depends on us; but note that that which depends on us does not feature at all in any of the reports of the Idle Argument.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:8531-8535] (Bobzien 1998, p. 181)

evidence.quote: The Stoics (and the Middle Platonists) considered the Idle Argument as a sophism.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:8712-8713] (Bobzien 1998, p. 185)

evidence.quote: one can certainly say that it contains various sophistic elements or lends itself to be interpreted as a fallacy.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:9338-9339] (Bobzien 1998, p. 198)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_the_idle_argu.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 8520-8527 (p. 181). Two misreadings. (a) 'a serious challenge to Stoic compatibilism': for Bobzien the argument 'is levelled against fate-determinism' and concerns the futility of action; 'that which depends on us does not feature at all in any of the reports', and the refutation 'is not a defence of free-will'. (b) 'not merely a sophism but a substantive philosophical position': the Stoics and Middle Platonists 'considered the Idle Argument as a sophism', and Bobzien's own verdict (§5.1.4) is that it 'contains various sophistic elements or lends itself to be interpreted as a fallacy'; what is substantive is Chrysippus' refutation, which elaborates his theory's 'concepts of causal relevance and intentional action'. The simply/co-fated summary is fine. page_range 'Chapter 5' = pp. 180-233.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_to_eph_hemin_.description: In §6.3.5 Bobzien separates two early Stoic concepts. 'What happens because of us' is 'one-sided' and 'causative': the 'we' names a necessary causal factor, and Chrysippus shows its compatibility with fate (it is a subclass of what is fated). 'What depends on us / is in our power' she assumes to be two-sided and potestative — a capacity for either walking or not walking, absent external force — readable in a way 'neutral with respect to determinism and indeterminism'; Chrysippus treats it as a necessary condition for moral responsibility, and the sources rule out an indeterminist reading. The 'through us (by fate)' formula is PHILOPATOR's later account.

evidence.quote: I assume that in our context the phrase was generally used to denote a two-sided, potestative concept of depend- ing on someone—a use that is well-attested
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:13115-13117] (Bobzien 1998, p. 281)

evidence.quote: this does not usually denote a two- sided, potestative, concept of dependency, but a one-sided causative one.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:13235-13236] (Bobzien 1998, p. 284, on 'happens because of us')

evidence.quote: There is a short version of it, 'that which happens through us', and a long version, 'that which happens through us by fate'.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:17586-17588] (Bobzien 1998, p. 378, PHILOPATOR's account)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_to_eph_hemin_.finding: No quote_verbatim; page_range 196-197 is wrong (that is §5.1.4). The node collapses three things Bobzien keeps apart in §6.3.5 (pp. 276-290): (1) 'happens because of us' (Greek para c. acc. / ek c. gen., trans. 'because of us') — this is the phrase she calls 'one-sided' and 'causative' for Chrysippus; (2) 'depends on us' / 'in our power' (eph' hemin / in nostra potestate), which she assumes 'was generally used to denote a two-sided, potestative concept', with a reading 'neutral with respect to determinism and indeterminism', and which Chrysippus treated as a necessary condition for moral responsibility; (3) 'that which happens through us (by fate)' — the dia-formula — which is PHILOPATOR's later Stoic account (§8.4, p. 378), not early Stoic. So 'one-sided and causative, meaning that which happens through us (di' hemon)' misassigns both the phrase and the property to eph' hemin and to the early Stoa; 'not indeterminist' is right.

scholarly_argument_bobzien_will_not_from.description: In the Introduction Bobzien brackets the history of the concept of the will from her subject: although 'clearly related to the problem of determinism and freedom', 'the development of the concept of the will did not spring from the discussion of early Stoic determinism and freedom' (n. 27 cites, as examples, Gilbert 1963, Voelke 1973, Dihle 1982, Kahn 1988). She does not deny that the early Stoic concept of assent and, in its wake, the Epictetan concept of prohairesis are essential both for the development of the concept of the will and for the compatibility problem; she treats them where required (6.3.3-6, 8.7) without aiming at comprehensiveness.

evidence.quote: However, as I see it, the development of the concept of the will did not spring from the discussion of early Stoic determinism and freedom.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:836-838] (Bobzien 1998, p. 13)

evidence.quote: e.g. Gilbert 1963, Voelke 1973, Dihle 1982, Kahn 1988.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Bobzien - 2001 - Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy.md:856] (Bobzien 1998, p. 13 n. 27)

scholarly_argument_bobzien_will_not_from.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at lines 834-844 (all on printed p. 13; n. 27 at line 856 reads exactly 'e.g. Gilbert 1963, Voelke 1973, Dihle 1982, Kahn 1988'; p. 14 begins at line 858). The first two sentences of the description are faithful and precise. The final sentence — 'The claim demarcates her project from studies, such as Voelke's, that read the Stoic theory of action as a doctrine of will' — is an inference not in the text: Bobzien lists Voelke 1973 only as one example ('e.g.') of the literature on the concept of the will and characterizes none of the four works. That over-claim confines the verdict to the last sentence; drop it or mark it as the node's own gloss.

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_cyclical_.description: Boys-Stones adduces the Platonist belief in exact cyclical recurrence (ps.-Plutarch, De fato 569A-C; Celsus apud Origen, Contra Celsum 5.21) as 'one extra piece of evidence' for his reading of hypothetical fate as 'a matter of perspective rather than substance'. Given the instantiated laws of nature, 'there is an absolute inevitability to their future progress; in identical circumstances, identical events will occur'; it therefore becomes 'impossible to think that Platonists advocated indeterminacy'. He does not rank this as the strongest evidence, and the phrase 'web of causes' is not his.

evidence.quote: I have one extra piece of evidence. This is the idea, apparently shared by a number of Platonists, that world history repeats itself precisely and eternally.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:412-415] (printed p. 442)

evidence.quote: Given the particular instantiation of the natural laws that the confluence of reason and necessity produced, there is an absolute inevitability to their future progress; in identical circumstances, identical events will occur.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:393-395] (printed p. 443, right column)

evidence.quote: If he is right—and ps.-Plutarch confirms that he is—it becomes impossible to think that Platonists advocated indeterminacy, or that this formed any part of their answer to the Stoics.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:444-446] (printed p. 444)

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_cyclical_.finding: The substance (exact recurrence rules out indeterminacy and confirms that the General Causal Principle operates) is in the article. But (a) the phrase 'web of causes', presented in quotation marks, does not occur anywhere in the author's text (rg 'web of causes' = 0 hits; it comes from the Claude-made summary in Extractions_articles, p. 443 attribution fabricated); (b) the author calls the cyclical-return argument 'one extra piece of evidence', not the 'strongest' evidence; (c) 'accepted determinism' is not his wording — he speaks of the General Causal Principle, 'absolute inevitability' and denial of 'indeterminacy'.

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_general_c.description: Boys-Stones finds 'no evidence that any Platonist of the period had any desire to deny the General Causal Principle in their efforts to save human autonomy' (p. 440). 'Within the cosmos, at least, the General Causal Principle still obtains' (p. 442) — the generation of the cosmos itself excepted, since the set of sublunary individuals is 'literally, the product of chance' (p. 441) — so Platonists did not advocate 'indeterminacy' (p. 444). His vocabulary is 'General Causal Principle', 'human autonomy', 'indeterminacy'; he never calls the Platonists determinists or uses 'libertarian'.

evidence.quote: There is, in general, no evidence that any Platonist of the period had any desire to deny the General Causal Principle in their efforts to save human autonomy. Our evidence is only that they did not believe it could be done on Stoic premises.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:314-317] (printed p. 440)

evidence.quote: Everything (except of course the generation of the cosmos itself, which necessarily cannot be conceived as happening within the rules that its generation entails) is the consequence according to the rules that govern the cosmos of something. Within the cosmos, at least, the General Causal Principle still obtains.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:396-400] (printed p. 442)

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_general_c.finding: The acceptance of the General Causal Principle is faithful (pp. 440-442, 444). But the label 'causal determinists, not libertarians' imports vocabulary the author never uses ('libertarian' = 0 hits; 'determinism' is used only of the Stoics and in cited titles). It also drops his explicit qualification: the Principle holds 'within the cosmos, at least', the generation of the cosmos itself excepted, and the set of sublunary individuals is 'the product of chance'. Page 438 concerns the Stoic reconciliation of fate and responsibility, not the Platonists.

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_justin_ma.description: Boys-Stones explicitly counts 'the Christian Justin' among the 'thinkers who provide evidence for the theory' of hypothetical fate, alongside Plutarch, Apuleius, Amelius and Alexander of Lycopolis (pp. 433-434); n. 9 refers to 1 Apology 43 'with C. Andresen, Justin und der mittlere Platonismus, ZNW 44 (1952-1953) 157-95, especially 183-88'. He does not characterise Justin's arguments or their relation to Alcinous; any claim about a Justin/Alcinous parallel belongs to Andresen and must be cited from Andresen.

evidence.quote: Other thinkers who provide evidence for the theory include Plutarch himself,8 the
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:64] (printed p. 433, right column)

evidence.quote: Christian Justin,9 Apuleius,10 Plotinus’ contemporary Amelius,
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:124] (printed p. 434)

evidence.quote: Cf. anyway I Apology 43 with C. Andresen, ‘Justin und der mittlere Platonismus’, Zeitschrift fur Neutestamentliche Wissenschaft 44 (1952-1953), 157-95, especially 183-88
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:137-139] (printed p. 434 n. 9)

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_justin_ma.finding: Two problems. (1) 'Implicitly' understates the text: in the body (pp. 433-434) Boys-Stones explicitly lists 'the Christian Justin' among the 'thinkers who provide evidence for the theory' of hypothetical fate, n. 9 giving 'Cf. anyway I Apology 43 with C. Andresen ... especially 183-88'. (2) The second clause — Justin's anti-heimarmene arguments 'closely parallel to Alcinous' — is nowhere in Boys-Stones; it is Andresen's content, imported by the Extractions_articles summary. The author says nothing about the substance of the Justin/Alcinous relation. That claim must be cited from Andresen (Extractions_articles/Andresen_1953_JustinMiddlePlatonism.md), not from this page.

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_middle_pl.description: Boys-Stones does not discuss 'free will' (the phrase appears only in cited titles). His thesis: Platonists of the period 'have no reason to be any less committed to the operation of the General Causal Principle within the cosmos than the Stoics'; what saves 'human ownership of their actions' is that 'chance, not god, is ultimately responsible for the existence of the individuals there are' (p. 441) — the consequence of two causal streams, transcendent divine providence and pre-existing matter (p. 440). 'Hypothetical fate' is thus 'a matter of perspective rather than substance' (p. 442).

evidence.quote: On the account I have given, Platonists have no reason to be any less committed to the operation of the General Causal Principle within the cosmos than the Stoics. It is enough for them that chance, not god, is ultimately responsible for the existence of the individuals there are to save human ownership of their actions.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:362-365] (printed p. 441, right column)

evidence.quote: But in case my claim that ‘hypothetical fate’ is really a matter of perspective rather than substance should seem to be placing an artificial construction on evidence
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:408-410] (printed p. 442)

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_middle_pl.finding: The first clause attributes to the author a thesis he never states: 'free will' occurs only inside two cited titles (Winston, 'Philo's doctrine of free will', line 147; Dillon's 'Fate and Freewill', line 152); there is no discussion of a 'modern sense' of free will. The article's vocabulary is 'human autonomy', 'to eph' hemin', 'ownership of action'. The second clause (General Causal Principle accepted within the cosmos, autonomy preserved through the two-causal-stream metaphysics) is faithful to pp. 440-442, but 'universal causal determinism' drops the 'within the cosmos' qualification.

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_primary_c.description: Boys-Stones holds that Platonists of the period wanted to 'save human ownership of their actions' (p. 441) and that their arguments against Stoic fate are 'essentially ad hominem': not that autonomy and antecedent causality are incompatible, but that Stoic physics, with god coextensive with matter as the single source of causality, makes 'god responsible for everything' (pp. 439-440, 446) — an idea 'impious' and 'theologically absurd' (p. 438). Platonists present Stoicism as 'a Plato without the metaphysics' (p. 445). He does not say their concern was 'not primarily' moral responsibility, nor speak of a 'problem of evil' or of matter's resistance.

evidence.quote: But the idea that god might be responsible for evil is not only impious, it is also theologically absurd (cf. SVF Π.1115), and perhaps metaphysically incoherent
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:250-252] (printed p. 438)

evidence.quote: All that Plutarch can argue is that the Stoics did not have the mechanism to make good their promise to effect the conjunction.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:313-314] (printed p. 440)

evidence.quote: we might summarize the attack by saying that the Stoics were bound to make god responsible for everything the moment they made him the single fount-head of all causal activity.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:510-512] (printed p. 446)

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_primary_c.finding: The sentence the node rests on ('The Platonists' concern is not primarily with the threat that Stoic determinism poses to human moral responsibility. It is, rather, with ... the problem of evil', p. 444) does not exist in the article: rg 'problem of evil', 'not primarily', 'resist' = 0 hits; 'evil' occurs once (p. 438), 'moral respons-' once (p. 438, about the Stoics). Section 7 (pp. 444-445) is about ps.-Plutarch 574D-F and the Platonist self-alignment against the Stoa. The author in fact says the Platonists wanted to 'save human ownership of their actions' (p. 441); their lever is theological — Stoic physics makes god 'responsible for everything' (pp. 440, 447), which is 'impious' and 'theologically absurd' (p. 438). No thesis about evils resulting from matter's resistance appears.

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_three_lev.description: Boys-Stones doubts that the 'doctrine of threefold providence' is original: ps.-Plutarch is 'the principal witness to three' but 'talks as if he is himself extending the term to the third level', with no near-contemporary support (only Nemesius much later) (p. 446). The operative point is the distinction between god's providence and that of the heavens: since Stoics identify nature, fate and providence, Platonists concede 'let nature be providence' but as a 'secondary providence', restoring 'the supremely providential role of the Demiurge' (pp. 446-447). Ps.-Plutarch's 'tertiary' providence may be a Sorites aimed at the Stoics (p. 447).

scholarly_argument_boys_stones_two_sourc.description: Where the Stoics take god to be coextensive with matter, so that 'everything is due to god', the Platonist world is 'the product not of one, but of two causal streams': divine providence which transcends the world, and matter which (at least conceptually) predates it (p. 440). God remains 'the ultimate explanatory cause of the ordered cosmos as such' and of the laws of nature instantiated by fate; but he is 'not directly responsible' for the sublunary individuals that result from applying those laws to matter — 'the set of individuals that populates the world is, literally, the product of chance' (p. 441).

evidence.quote: For the Platonist world is the product not of one, but of two causal streams. One is associated with divine providence which transcends the world; the other with matter which (at least conceptually) predates it.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Middle_Platonists_on_Fate_and_Human_Aut_OCR.md:349-353] (printed p. 440)

evidence.quote: god (the demiurge or divine intellect) is the ultimate explanatory cause of the ordered cosmos as such (which means that he is responsible for the laws of nature, which is the law instantiated by fate), he is not directly responsible for any of the individuals

evidence.quote: In fact, no-one at all in this sense is directly responsible: the set of individuals that populates the world is, literally, the product of chance.

The phrase 'chance encounter' is not his either.

scholarly_argument_dihle_augustine_s_inv.description: Dihle accepts the general view, and asserts it himself, that St. Augustine 'invented' the notion of will used as a tool of analysis from the Scholastics to Nietzsche. Augustine knew the Neoplatonic (Porphyrian) triad used by Marius Victorinus but did not apply it to the Trinity; he approached will from the Biblical belief that man is God's image and, 'quite against the philosophical tradition', applied introspection and self-analysis to the image of the Trinity, so that Trinitarian theology and human psychology became directly related. The shared ontological premises had previously precluded transferring 'will' to anthropology.

evidence.quote: the notion of will, as it is used as a tool of analysis and description in many philosophical doctrines from the early Scholas-tics to Schopenhauer and Nietzsche,' was invented by St. Augustine.
evidence.citation: [Albrecht Dihle - The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures) (1982, University of California Press).md:5425-5428] (Dihle 1982, p. 123)

evidence.quote: These fundamen-tal assumptions precluded the transference of the notion of will, which had been invented ro attain an adequate description of the unfolding of reality, from theology and ontology to the field of Biblical anthropol-ogy, ethics, and soteriology.
evidence.citation: [Albrecht Dihle - The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures) (1982, University of California Press).md:5445-5448] (Dihle 1982, p. 123)

evidence.quote: But St. Augustine's attempt to verify the similarity by dis-covering the points of direct reference on both sides was quite against the philosophical tradition. He attempted to apply what he had per-ceived by means of introspection and self-analysis to the image of the Trinity.
evidence.citation: [Albrecht Dihle - The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures) (1982, University of California Press).md:5503-5508] (Dihle 1982, pp. 124-125)

scholarly_argument_dihle_augustine_s_inv.finding: The opening sentence of ch. The Biblical-anthropology (Gen 1:27), introspection and Trinity/psychology elements are on pp. 124-125. But the node says Augustine drew 'on Biblical anthropology ... and Neoplatonic ontology through introspection', which flattens Dihle's contrast: on pp. 123-124 the shared Neoplatonic/Christian ontological premises are what 'precluded the transference of the notion of will ... to the field of Biblical anthropology', and Augustine's introspective method was 'quite against the philosophical tradition'; unlike Victorinus he 'did not use the Porphyrian triad' to explain the Trinity. Dihle does say (p. 144) Augustine worked 'in continuation of' the Greek Trinitarian theologians, so the relation is continuation-plus-break, not a drawing-on. The word 'formally' is not Dihle's. page_range '5425-5428, 5494-5511' are .md line numbers, not printed pages: printed pp. 123-125 (and 144).

scholarly_argument_dihle_historical_deve.description: Dihle closes ch. I by stating that the 'clear-cut notion of will' — will as a factor separate from both reason and emotion or instinct — was always implied in the Biblical image of God, man and the universe, yet utterly alien to Greek cosmology and ethics; it took a very long time before it was conceived 'by the means and methods of Greek philosophy' (the story of Paul, Philo, the Greek theologians and finally Augustine in the later chapters).

scholarly_argument_dihle_historical_deve.finding: Quote located verbatim at lines 979-982, printed p. 19 (end of ch. The description's 'distinct, arbitrary faculty separate from reason' imports 'arbitrary' (Galen's word for the Jewish creator's intention, p. 1) into Dihle's definition of will; Dihle's own gloss (p. 20) is 'will as a factor separate from both reason and emotion or instinct'. scholarly_argument_dihle_jewish_and_chri.description: Dihle opens with Galen's digression (De usu partium): according to Galen, the Jews derive the universe exclusively from the arbitrary intention of the creator, who can turn a lump of earth into a horse or a bird — an opinion Galen judges preferable to Epicurus' chance but incompatible with Greek cosmology as expounded by Plato and Aristotle. Dihle himself adds (p. 4) that Biblical cosmology admits no rule binding creator and creation alike: creation results from the power and pleasure or will of Yahveh and from nothing else. This contrast frames the whole inquiry into 'will'.

But the passage is Dihle's report of Galen's digression in De usu partium: 'The Jews, he says, derive...'; 'This opinion, according to Galen, is certainly preferable to the aleatoric conception of Epicurus'. The node turns reported speech into Dihle's own assertions: (a) the 'preferable to Epicurean chance' judgement is Galen's, not Dihle's; (b) 'early Christian theology' is not in the passage — Galen speaks of the Jews, and Dihle of 'the Biblical concept of creation' (p. 3) and 'Biblical cosmology' (p. 4). scholarly_argument_dihle_paul_s_concept_.description: For Dihle, Paul's teaching implies a will of man distinguished both from all intellectual achievements (even knowledge of the divine Law) and from unconscious, spontaneous emotions: a will that responds to God's commandment, determines action and is therefore subject to divine and moral judgement. Fulfilling the Law is primarily an act of obedience, testifying to will rather than intellect. Paul had no term for this ('no such term in the language of St. Paul and his contemporaries'), though the underlying concept is 'quite clear'; Dihle adds that its impact on the next two or three centuries of Christian theology 'was not too heavy'.

evidence.quote: for it is, in his view, a will, as distinguished from all intellectual achievements—even with regard to the knowledge of the divine Law— as well as from all unconscious and spontaneous emotions, which re-sponds to the commandment of God.
evidence.citation: [Albrecht Dihle - The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures) (1982, University of California Press).md:3721-3724] (Dihle 1982, p. 83)

evidence.citation: [Albrecht Dihle - The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures) (1982, University of California Press).md:3589-3590] (Dihle 1982, p. 80)

evidence.citation: [Albrecht Dihle - The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity (Sather Classical Lectures) (1982, University of California Press).md:3703-3704] (Dihle 1982, p. 83)

scholarly_argument_dihle_paul_s_concept_.finding: Quote located verbatim at lines 3719-3727, printed p. 83. Dihle: Paul's will is 'distinguished from all intellectual achievements ... as well as from all unconscious and spontaneous emotions', it 'responds to the commandment of God' and 'determines human action'; 'There is no such term in the language of St. Paul'; 'The underlying concept, however, is quite clear'. scholarly_argument_eliasson_alexander_of.description: Eliasson finds in Alexander's De fato one clear development of the Aristotelian notion of eph' hemin: where Aristotle is vague between an inclusive and an exclusive notion, Alexander explicitly opts for the exclusive one, defining what depends on us as what comes about with an unforced assent in accordance with reason and judgment (De fato 183.26-32), and this move underlies his 'perhaps innovative' association of the notion with choice — though Alexander only associates it with choice and never says choice itself is eph' hemin. Eliasson notes (n. 110) that De fato must counter Stoic criticism unknown to Aristotle.

evidence.quote: On the other hand we do find something in Alexander that clearly constitutes a development in the Aristotelian notion of τ φ’ μν. Unlike Aristotle, who is vague as to whether the notion of φ’ μν is to be understood in what we have called the inclusive or exclusive way, Alexander in fact explicitly opts for an exclusive notion
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:4048-4052] (Eliasson 2008, p. 74)

evidence.quote: Thus, Alexander never to my knowledge goes as far as saying that ‘choosing’ is φ’ μν. This simply is not the way he uses the notion.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:4045-4047] (Eliasson 2008, p. 74)

evidence.quote: Alexander, on the contrary, clearly develops an exclusive notion of φ’ μν, defining it as what comes about with an unforced assent that is in accordance with reason and judgment.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:11361-11363] (Eliasson 2008, p. 218)

scholarly_argument_eliasson_alexander_of.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at p. 74 (Greek dropped in the extraction exactly as in the node). Page range 72-79 = section 3.4 (conclusions 3.5 run to p. 80). But the description replaces Eliasson's actual point with a generic frame: he never speaks of 'contingency'; what he identifies as the development is that Alexander 'explicitly opts for an exclusive notion', spelled out as what comes about with an unforced assent in accordance with reason and judgment, and that this move lies behind his 'perhaps innovative association of the notion with choice' — while insisting Alexander only associates the notion with choice and never says choice is eph' hemin. The anti-Stoic context is only a footnote caveat (n. 110: De fato 'must counter mainly Stoic criticism of Aristotle'; p. 72: a problem 'unknown to Aristotle').

scholarly_argument_eliasson_aristotle_s_.description: Eliasson holds that Aristotle's notion of eph' hemin, central to the preconditions of virtue in EN III, is 'unclear': the condition that the origin is in the agent is vague, so Aristotle employs both what Eliasson calls an exclusive notion (tied to rational agents and their activities alone) and an inclusive notion (not tied to rational agency alone). Aristotle applies the notion equally to actions and to internal states (character states, affections, thoughts, reasonings), and his account of deliberation adds a 'tentative' ontological basis not present in ordinary-language uses.

evidence.quote: his notion is still unclear in a way which poses problems for its interpretation. The basic unclarity consists in that he employs both what we have called an exclusive notion of φ’ μν, related to a notion of action on which all actions, including actions that are φ’ μν, are rational actions
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:3306-3310] (Eliasson 2008, p. 60)

evidence.quote: The inclusive refers to the notion being in no way tied to rational agency alone. The exclusive refers to the notion being applied to rational agents and their activities alone.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:4335-4337] (Eliasson 2008, p. 80)

evidence.quote: Aristotle applies the notion of φ’ μν equally not only to actions (πρ*ξεις) but to internal states of the agent as well
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:3290-3291] (Eliasson 2008, p. 60)

scholarly_argument_eliasson_aristotle_s_.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at p. 60 (section 3.1.5); pages 47-60 = section 3.1 (ends p. 61). Internal states (3.1.4, p. 57-60) and 'tentative ontology' (3.1.3, p. 52) are Eliasson's own headings. Two losses: (1) Eliasson does not say Aristotle 'developed' two notions — the inclusive/exclusive pair is a distinction he introduces to capture a 'basic unclarity' / 'vagueness' in Aristotle's condition that the origin is in the agent; (2) the pair is defined by rational agency (inclusive = 'in no way tied to rational agency alone'; exclusive = rational agents and their activities alone), not by 'all voluntary actions'.

scholarly_argument_eliasson_chrysippus_a.description: For Eliasson, Chrysippus' notion of eph' hemin (applied to internal acts of assent and impulse, and to external actions) rests on his account of causes and their fatedness: auxiliary external causes do not by themselves explain an action, which also requires reference to the agent's nature as expressed in his assent; the notion thus identifies the agent's contribution to the causation of his actions, within a defence of the compatibility of the theory of fate with a common notion of what depends on us. Eliasson largely agrees with Bobzien 1998a, only slightly modifying two points.

evidence.quote: One fairly recent and substantial view that we have reasons to largely agree with is the one defended in Bobzien (1998a).
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:4534-4535] (Eliasson 2008, p. 84)

evidence.quote: In what follows I will agree with most of this. Still, the textual basis, I take it, will demand that we slightly modify or specify (i) as well as (iv).

evidence.quote: Thus, Chrysippus’ notion of φ’ μν is one that seeks to identify the contribution made by agents to the causation of their actions. This feature vanishes in the Roman Stoa.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:6247-6249] (Eliasson 2008, p. 116)

scholarly_argument_eliasson_chrysippus_a.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at p. 116 (section 4.6). The first sentence's content (causes/fatedness, auxiliary causes, agent's nature expressed in assent) is faithful; 'compatibilism' is attested in Eliasson only in n. 14 (p. 84, 'Chrysippus’ compatibilism'), elsewhere he says 'compatibility'. The second sentence misreads his stance: the 'recent interpretation' (4.1.1) is Bobzien 1998a, with which Eliasson says 'we have reasons to largely agree' and 'I will agree with most of this', proposing only to 'slightly modify or specify' points (i) and (iv). He also adopts from Bobzien the view that the issue was the agent's autonomy as cause, not alternative possibilities. 'Requires careful re-examination' is not his position.

scholarly_argument_eliasson_middle_plato.description: Eliasson discerns a standard Middle-Platonist notion of eph' hemin, found in Alcinous, Ps.-Plutarch, Nemesius, Calcidius, Apuleius (with reservations) and Maximus of Tyre: all things are included in fate, but what depends on us is included hypothetically, neither fated nor necessary, while its consequences are fated — an account inspired by hints in Plato, with a modal taxonomy drawn from Aristotle's EN III. The early Philo (no account of fate; exclusive notion tied to praise and blame) and Plutarch (tripartition fate/chance/eph' hemin) are the exceptions to this standard view.

evidence.quote: As examples of such exceptions, e.g. the early Philo of Alexandria does not connect the notion of φ’ μν to an account of fate, but the issue is often simply the proper analysis of the basis of moral praise and blame.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:8817-8820] (Eliasson 2008, p. 166)

evidence.quote: With these two exceptions in mind, the elements of the standard Middle-Platonist account become more clear. In the main sources for this account analyzed above, Alcinous’ Didascalicus, Ps.-Plutarch’s De fato, Nemesius of Emesa’s De natura hominis, Calcidius’ In Timaeum, Apuleius’ De Platone,201 and Maximus of Tyre’s Orations, the main idea is that all things are included in fate.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:8834-8839] (Eliasson 2008, p. 166)

evidence.quote: As we have seen, this account was inspired by some hints in various Platonic passages, rather than any complete Platonic theory of the matter.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:8862-8864] (Eliasson 2008, p. 167)

scholarly_argument_eliasson_middle_plato.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at p. 166; the quote itself already says 'several authors that constitute interesting exceptions to this standard view'. The description lists Philo and Plutarch among the sources in which the standard notion 'is visible', whereas Eliasson names exactly these two as the exceptions: the early Philo does not connect the notion to an account of fate at all (exclusive notion tied to praise and blame), and Plutarch works with a tripartition of causes that excludes eph' hemin from fate. The standard account is found in Alcinous, Ps.-Plutarch, Nemesius, Calcidius, Apuleius (with a caveat, n. 201) and Maximus. 'Responding to Stoic and Peripatetic developments' is also not his framing: the account was 'inspired by some hints in various Platonic passages', with the modal taxonomy drawing on Aristotle's EN III.

scholarly_argument_eliasson_plotinus_s_n.description: In chapter 6 Eliasson re-reads every occurrence of eph' hemin and of epi + dative of person in the Enneads — first outside VI.8 (III.1, I.4, III.2), then within VI.8 — in the light of his study of the Aristotelian, Stoic and Middle-Platonist background, in order to state what Plotinus criticizes, what he adopts, and what he achieves. Outside VI.8 the notion 'clearly tends towards an exclusive notion', restricted to what involves a specific rational activity and truly has its principle in us.

evidence.quote: Now, then, we are more able to say something specific on how Plotinus’ notion relates to this tradition, i.e. what more specifically it is that he criticizes, what he adopts in his own account, and what he achieves by his own analysis.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:8956-8959] (Eliasson 2008, p. 170)

evidence.quote: Plotinus’ notion of φ’ μν outside Ennead VI.8 clearly tends towards an exclusive notion, i.e. one in which only some things, namely those that involve a specific rational activity, and in a true sense have their principle in us, are φ’ μν.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:11270-11273] (Eliasson 2008, p. 215)

scholarly_argument_eliasson_plotinus_s_n.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at p. 170 (chapter 6 intro). The description is generic and partly imported: Eliasson's programme is to analyse, 'in the light of the results of the study of the background', all occurrences in the Enneads — both outside and within VI.8 — in order to say 'what more specifically it is that he criticizes, what he adopts in his own account, and what he achieves by his own analysis'. The node restricts the claim to occurrences outside VI.8 and adds 'in his metaphysical framework', which is not his phrase; the actual result for the treatises outside VI.8 (a notion that 'clearly tends towards an exclusive notion') is missing. page_range '169-' is open-ended; chapter 6 runs pp. 169-216.

scholarly_argument_eliasson_that_which_d.description: Eliasson sorts previous readings of Plotinus' to eph' hemin into five kinds — the freedom, free choice, free will, free action and self-determination interpretations — and finds that the notion has seldom been treated as a separate issue, that readings are stipulated rather than argued, that there is no consensus on Plotinus' sources (Stoic, EN III, Alexander, Platonic), and that much confusion stems from the non-argued-for assumption that Plotinus and his predecessors discussed one general problem in different terms. His terminological, historical study of the pre-Plotinian tradition aims to come to terms with these problems.

evidence.quote: Rather, as a rule, people tend to simply stipulate their own readings of the notion without taking into account the fact that other people have diﬀerent readings of it.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:1692-1694] (Eliasson 2008, p. 27)

evidence.quote: The present study thus aims at coming to terms with some of these problems, by analyzing the notions of φ’ μν in the diﬀerent schools within the tradition of writings on φ’ μν preceding Plotinus.
evidence.citation: [[Philosophia Antiqua 113] Erik Eliasson - The Notion of That Which Depends on Us in Plotinus and Its Background (Philosophia Antiqua - Volume 113) (2008, Brill Academic Publishers).md:2489-2491] (Eliasson 2008, p. 43)

scholarly_argument_eliasson_that_which_d.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at p. 42 (section 2.4). The five labels (freedom, free choice, free will, free action, self-determination) are Eliasson's own groupings of previous scholarship (2.3.1-2.3.5, pp. 27-42). But he does not say they are 'all inadequate or partial': his diagnosis is that the notion has not been treated as a separate issue, that interpreters 'simply stipulate their own readings' without arguing against others, that there is 'no consensus' on sources, and that confusion derives from the 'non-argued-for assumption' that Plotinus and his predecessors discussed one general problem. The terminological approach is motivated in 1.3 (p. 14) and 2.4 as a way to come to terms with 'some of these problems', not stated as strictly 'necessary'.

This biblical freedom is religious-'theokratisch', not a concept of human self-determination; responsibility surfaces 'in einem deterministischen Zusammenhang' as a 'Miteinander und Ineinander' of divine and human action. Ezekiel 18 is a 'Plädoyer für die Eigenverantwortung', collective ('nationale') yet also individual, plus the permanent possibility of conversion.

scholarly_argument_f_rst_early_christian.description: Fürst: from the mid-2nd century Christian Platonists shared the Platonic critique of Stoic Kompatibilismus but, with unprecedented 'Vehemenz', called τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν and τὸ αὐτεξούσιον 'frei' and ascribed freedom of self-determination to every human as natural endowment — a 'Freiheitspathos' that made freedom an 'Eckpfeiler' of Christian thought. Justin (Apol. I 43 f.) was the first expressly to proclaim the 'Freiheit der Entscheidung', with only a brief theoretical grounding; the apologists offered no developed theories. Clement laid the 'Grundstein' of a philosophy of freedom by opposing freedom (ἐξουσία) to fixed nature (οὐσία); Origen first systematised.

scholarly_argument_f_rst_free_will_termi.description: Fürst's terminological caution: no concept of 'Wille' existed before Augustine, so he largely avoids the word and stays close to the ancient terms — προαίρεσις (Aristotle's 'überlegtes Streben', not 'freie Wahl'), τὸ ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν ('das, was an uns liegt', whose rendering as 'Wille/Freiheit/Willensfreiheit' is 'ausgeprochen irreführend'), and the later τὸ αὐτεξούσιον ('Selbstmächtigkeit'). His subject is freedom in the ethical, not political, sense. He nevertheless deploys the modern labels Determinismus, Kompatibilismus and Libertarismus as analytic categories throughout.

He does not label these positions 'libertarisch' nor rank them by sophistication.

The telos 'Gott alles in allem' (1 Cor 15:28) is reached 'über die Freiheit', by persuasion, 'nicht durch Zwang und Gewalt'. Yet Fürst flags that this Telosformel, together with divine foreknowledge and pre-arrangement, raises the problem whether the 'durch und durch libertarische Konzept' finally issues in a Determinismus — a tension he settles only as 'Libertarist mit kompatibilistischen Neigungen'.

scholarly_argument_meyer_aristotle_on_pr.description: Meyer leaves prohairesis untranslated: it 'captures the general phenomenon of doing something for a reason', is a determinate decision informed by deliberation, and 'rather than one's action best reveals one's character' (the goal for the sake of which one acts). For praise and blame, however, 'voluntariness rather than prohairesis is the central notion'. Aristotle's two criteria for the voluntary are that the action 'originate' in the agent (the agent moves his own bodily parts) and that the agent know 'the particulars' of the action; ignorance of the good does not make an action involuntary.

scholarly_argument_meyer_aristotle_on_pr.finding: The voluntary-action half is faithful: origin in the agent (L3870-3873, p. 71) and knowledge of 'the particulars' (L3893-3895, p. 71). The prohairesis half is not Meyer's position. She also warns against reading 'moral responsibility' into Aristotle: praiseworthiness depends on the goodness of actions and motivations, not on 'whether we are responsible for them' (pp. 70-71), and Aristotle is 'quite innocent' of the modern assumption linking responsibility for character to responsibility for action (p. 86). scholarly_argument_meyer_aristotle_on_re.description: Meyer reads EN III 5 as a 'very simple' argument: we become just or unjust by our actions, and we know this while performing the character-forming actions, so we 'voluntarily become the sorts of people we are'. The modern objection from deprived upbringing misfires: Aristotle does not assume we are responsible for knowing right from wrong, only that his well-educated audience does know it; he is not claiming responsibility 'no matter what the circumstances'. The responsibility he defends is 'at best partial' ('co-causes in a way', 1114b23), and voluntariness interests him as an expression, not a source, of character.

Aristotle, however, starts from a much weaker assumption: that we do in fact know this.

scholarly_argument_meyer_aristotle_on_we.description: On Meyer's reading Aristotle stands in the tradition of Plato's Socrates in the Protagoras: knowing what one should do is impossible without properly cultivated desires, so in EN VII 1-3 he agrees with Socrates that the acratic (weak-willed) and encratic (self-controlled) person, whose desires conflict with reason, 'do not fully know' that this is the right thing to do. Aristotle accepts the Platonic premise that wrongdoing results from ethical ignorance; what he rejects is the inference that wrongdoing is therefore involuntary, since wrongdoing is blameworthy.

To think or know that something is good involves desiring and taking pleasure in it. This is why Aristotle, in his own discussion of acrasia (weakness of will) in EN VII 1–3 agrees with the Socrates of Plato’s Protagoras

scholarly_argument_meyer_plato_on_knowle.description: Meyer: on 'the view that emerges across Plato's dialogues', knowing or even believing that something is good requires desiring or taking pleasure in it; hence 'there is no such thing, on this view, as knowingly doing wrong'. We all want the good, so bad action 'must be explained by ignorance' (Laws 860d-861a); apparent cases of acting against one's knowledge under emotion are, Socrates argues in the Protagoras, really cases of ignorance. Meyer treats this as constant, adding that 'even in the Republic', despite the tripartite psyche, Socrates insists on it; she does not describe later dialogues as complicating it.

scholarly_argument_meyer_stoic_determini.description: Meyer deliberately does not discuss whether fated actions can be 'up to us' — 'an issue in their metaphysics and philosophy of nature'. She reports only that the Stoics disputed with contemporaries whether their thesis of fate ('a determinist thesis') undermined what is up to us; that for the earlier Stoics an action is up to me if the impulse causing it depends on my assent, so the actions of wise and foolish alike are up to them and 'praise and blame are appropriate only for what is up to us' (Gellius 7.2.6-13); and (n. 2) that the ancient dispute concerns internal versus external causes. No cylinder analogy appears.

scholarly_argument_meyer_stoic_freedom_a.description: Meyer's Appendix 1 separates two notions: the freedom (eleutheria) the Stoics attribute to the sage, contrasted with slavery and not with determinism, and 'what is up to us' (eph' hemin), disputed in the fate debate. Sage and fool are 'equally up to them', but only the wise are free. Epictetus links the two by holding that the only thing up to us is 'the correct use of impressions' — assenting only to correct impulsive impressions and so being without passions — thereby diverging from the earlier Stoics, for whom an action is up to me if its impulse depends on my assent. Even in Epictetus 'the issue of determinism is not at stake'.

evidence.quote: It is important not to mistake the freedom (eleutheria) that the Stoics contrast with slavery for another kind of ‘freedom’ which, in modern discussions, is often spoken of in contrast with determinism.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Susan Sauve Meyer - Ancient Ethics (2008).md:9515-9517] (Meyer 2008, p. 183)

evidence.quote: On their view, the actions of both the sage and the fool are equally ‘up to them’, but it is only the wise who are free.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Susan Sauve Meyer - Ancient Ethics (2008).md:9523-9524] (Meyer 2008, p. 183)

evidence.quote: In claiming that the only thing that is up to us is the correct use of impressions, Epictetus diverges from the earlier Stoic notion of ‘what is up to us’.
evidence.citation: [01_Philosophie_antique/Susan Sauve Meyer - Ancient Ethics (2008).md:9565-9567] (Meyer 2008, p. 184)

scholarly_argument_meyer_stoic_freedom_a.finding: quote_verbatim located verbatim at L9545-9564 (pp. 183-184). But 'compatibilist account of freedom' is imported vocabulary that contradicts the appendix's opening thesis: Stoic eleutheria, contrasted with slavery, must not be mistaken for the 'freedom' spoken of 'in contrast with determinism'; 'even here, the issue of determinism is not at stake'. Meyer uses 'compatibilism' only to name the modern issue she sets apart (n. 2). The node also merges two notions Meyer separates: the wise and the fool are 'equally up to them', yet only the wise are free; and 'the only thing up to us is the correct use of impressions' is Epictetus's view, which 'diverges from the earlier Stoic notion'. 'True freedom consists in following nature/reason' is a gloss; her formulation is 'neither hindered nor compelled' (p. 173) and eliminating the passions (p. 184).

scholarly_argument_meyer_stoic_passions_.description: Meyer: for the Stoics a passion 'is a judgment or belief', irrational 'in virtue of being false' — a false judgment about the good — and also an impulse; virtue requires the extirpation of all passions ('the wise man will be free from passions'). Stoic freedom means being 'neither hindered nor compelled'; because passions (unlike 'good feelings') expose one to impediment and compulsion, the doctrine that the sage is free from passions lies 'at the root' of the paradox that 'only the wise are free'. In Epictetus, correct assent that eliminates the passions is what achieves this freedom.

Maston does not call the Hodayot deterministic; he argues only that covenantal nomism cannot account for the spirit's role.

scholarly_argument_voelke_determinism_an.description: Voelke: the Stoic distinction between the cause 'perfect in itself' (perfecta et principalis) and merely auxiliary/antecedent causes reconciles human freedom with universal fatality. When the perfect cause lies in us, the action is 'in our power', which for the Stoics means it is free; assent to an impression is free although conditioned by an external impression, because it expresses the soul's own force and nature. Men are thus responsible for the evil they do, yet to be borne with patience. Voelke notes that Chrysippus' kataleptic-impression doctrine seriously compromises the freedom of assent (pp. 36-37).

scholarly_argument_voelke_free_will_in_s.description: Voelke: in Stoic rationalism 'reason is will'. Boulēsis (rational wish; Cicero's voluntas) is only one species of tendency; judgement (assent) and tendency are both derived forms of a primordial will that is tension (tonos), force, effort upon oneself. Stoic inner freedom is not 'libre arbitre' understood as the power to choose indifferently between two opposites, and the will is never freed from the cosmic order; but consent to Destiny is the voluntary act par excellence, and the sage realises an autonomy whose exercise is also the realisation of his own nature.

scholarly_argument_voelke_free_will_in_s.finding: Two misreadings. (a) The node equates Voelke's 'volonté' with boulēsis. For Voelke boulēsis (rational wish, Cicero's voluntas) is only one species of tendency (pp. 57-58); his thesis is that judgement and tendency are derived forms of a 'volonté primordiale qui est tension, force, effort sur soi-même' (p. 193) and that 'la raison est volonté' (p. 7). (b) 'rational assent to fate rather than autonomous choice' opposes what Voelke unites: consent to Destiny is the 'acte volontaire par excellence' by which we accede to freedom (pp. 97, 99); Epictetus' prohairesis is a 'choix primordial' and Voelke ends on 'l'autonomie du sage stoïcien' (p. 201). What Voelke does say (p. 146 n.) is that Stoic inner freedom is not 'libre arbitre' understood as the power to choose indifferently between two opposites — a narrower claim than the node's.

scholarly_argument_voelke_prohairesis_an.description: Voelke: in Epictetus (the old Stoics scarcely used the notion) the prohairesis is the primordial choice rooting our moral project — a power of judging, choosing and willing accompanied by reflexive consciousness, immanent to desire, tendency and assent rather than transcending them (against Marcus Aurelius). It is sometimes identified with the self ('le moi lui-même', 'personne morale') and is the principle of the only freedom we have, inner freedom, which is not a libre arbitre. Unlike Aristotle's prohairesis, where pro- marks preference, the Stoic definition gives the prefix a temporal value ('choix avant le choix').

scholarly_argument_voelke_prohairesis_an.finding: Voelke's claims are about Epictetus, not 'the Stoic prohairesis': the old Stoics 'ne paraissent pas avoir fait un ample usage de cette notion' (p. 144) and its 'mise en relief' is Epictetus' most notable novelty (p. 198). In Epictetus the prohairesis is 'parfois considérée comme le moi lui-même' (p. 153) and 'le principe de la seule liberté dont nous disposions, la liberté intérieure' (p. 198) — which Voelke explicitly says is not a libre arbitre (p. 146 n.). The Aristotle contrast is present (pp. 143-144: Aristotelian pro- marks preference, Stoic pro- temporal anteriority), but Voelke also notes Epictetus sometimes gives the prefix the comparative value (p. 147). Voelke's own gloss is 'pouvoir de juger, de choisir et de vouloir accompagné de conscience réflexive', not 'faculty of choice/assent'.
